body: 【ワシントン時事】11月3日の米中間選挙まで27日で1週間。トランプ大統領率いる与党共和党は、対イラン軍事作戦に伴う物価高で逆風にさらされている。野党民主党は共和党の地盤でも攻勢をかけており、下院では多数派を奪還するとの見方が広がる。上院は接戦が見込まれ、激戦7州の行方に注目が集まる。【ひと目でわかる】米中間選挙の情勢トランプ氏は25日、激戦となっている中西部ミシガン州で演説し「共和党が勝利すれば一人ひとりが5000ドル（約78万円）を手にし、かつてない経済的成功を収める」と改めて訴えた。共和党の苦戦が伝えられる中、トランプ氏は露骨な「ばらまき」政策を前面に出し、巻き返しに躍起となっている。選挙分析機関クック・ポリティカル・リポートの予測によると、下院（定数435）は民主党優勢の選挙区が220で、過半数の218を上回る。これに対し、共和党優勢の選挙区は198。接戦に位置付けられる17選挙区の多くは共和党が猛追を受ける展開で、同党は厳しい戦いを強いられている。35議席を争う上院（同100）は激しい攻防が続く。共和党の優勢選挙区は非改選を合わせ46、民主党は47で伯仲。接戦7州には共和党牙城の南部テキサス州や中西部カンザス州、民主党が議席を有するミシガン州が含まれ、勝敗の行方は最後まで見通せない。上下両院で多数派を握る共和党が劣勢に立たされる背景には、トランプ氏の人気低下がある。ロイター通信が19日に公表した世論調査によると、同氏の支持率は過去最低の31％に落ち込んだ。要因の一つはイラン作戦が招いたエネルギー価格の高騰で、ガソリン高などが家計を直撃し、国民の不満が高まっている。トランプ氏は連日遊説を重ねるが、共和党候補の中には政権による関税政策を批判するなど同氏と距離を置く動きも表面化している。一方、民主党はイラン作戦や物価高を争点に掲げ、共和党の牙城にも資金を投入。政権批判票の取り込みに全力を挙げている。

title: 茨城県教委 国に誤った情報伝達
body: 公益通報制度の運用状況を巡り、茨城県教育委員会が誤った情報を国に伝達していたことが、県教委への取材で明らかになった。担当者の誤解が原因で、是正件数に間違いがあったという。【図解で見る】都道府県の状況は?　内部通報、愛媛県は20年間ゼロ◇是正「31件」→実は「10件」消費者庁は制度の活用状況を把握するため、全国の自治体を対象として定期的に照会。2006年の制度開始以降、通報や是正の件数、通報窓口の設置状況などを調べている。茨城県教委は20年度分について、是正件数が31件だったと消費者庁に報告していたが、実際は10件だったことが判明。残る21件は是正件数ではなく、通報後の調査で不正が確認されなかった件数だったという。◇「一連の流れ、正しく理解を」毎日新聞の問い合わせなどを受けて県教委が確認したところ、誤りが判明。当時の担当者が通報から是正までの手続きを誤解したまま回答していたという。県教委に通報した経験がある元学校関係者は「これまでの対応を組織的に検証してほしい」と訴える。制度に詳しい淑徳大の日野勝吾教授は「誤った情報は調査全体に影響する」と指摘。「国は制度の趣旨や運用方法を改めて周知し、通報から是正までの一連の流れを正しく理解してもらう必要がある」と求める。消費者庁の担当者は「個別の事情にはコメントしないが、自治体が責任を持って報告していると考えている」と述べた。【古瀬弘治】

title: ながら運転で子奪われ10年 父は今
body:
愛知県一宮市で、『ポケモンGO』をしながら運転していた男のトラックに、小学生がひかれて死亡した事故から10年となりました。今もなくならない「ながら運転」の事故に、父親が思いを語りました。【動画で見る】運転中『ポケモンGO』のトラックに小学生の我が子の命奪われ10年 繰り返される“ながら運転”の悲劇に父親の思いは
10年前に撮影されたホームビデオ。楽しそうな表情を見せるのは、当時9歳の則竹敬太くんです。生きていれば、2026年11月を迎えるはずでした。父・則竹崇智さん：「もう生きていたよりも、亡くなってしまってからの方が、月日が長いんだなと思いながら、『父さん、今日も一日頑張ってくるから、見守っていてね』という思いで手を合わせました」父の崇智さんは、自宅から歩いて3分ほどのこの場所で、毎朝手を合わせます。
事故が起きたのは10年前の2016年10月26日。小学4年生だった敬太君は、学校からの下校途中、横断歩道を渡っていたところをトラックにひかれて命を落としました。原因は、運転手の「ながら運転」。位置情報を使ったスマホゲーム『ポケモンGO』で遊びながら、ハンドルを握っていました。
父・則竹崇智さん（2016年）：「『ポケモンGOかよ』というのが正直な気持ちです。本当に…誕生日ももうあとちょっとで10歳になって、楽しみにしていたのに、楽しいことが待っていたのに」運転とは関係のない“ゲームへの操作”が死亡事故に。過失運転致死の罪に問われたドライバーに言い渡された判決は、禁錮3年でした。父・則竹崇智さん：「男の子が2人生まれたから、長男が20歳になって敬太も20歳になって、男3人で一杯やれるなって、敬太が生まれた時に私が思っていたささやかな幸せ。男同士、杯が酌み交わせるなと思ったんですが、実現できなかったのは非常に残念です」
同じ悲しみを経験する人を一人でも減らしたい。崇智さんは、事故の悲惨さや命の尊さを伝える講演を続けています。父・則竹崇智さん：「ハッと気付いた時にはトラックは目の前。ちょうどボンネットの真ん中に、この水筒がドンッとぶつかります。数メートル飛ばされます。後方で見ていた長男が『敬太！バカバカバカバカ死ぬな死ぬな』って靴を拾い上げて、敬太のところに寄って行ったそうです」

title: 新iPad mini発表 防水を初搭載
body: 新しい折りたたみスマートフォン「iPhone Duo」を開くと、まるで「iPad mini」のようだ。それでも、やはり本物のiPad miniが欲しい人はいるだろう。そんな人に向けて、米アップルは新型iPad miniを11月6日に発売する。日本ではWi-Fiモデルが11万9800円（税込）から。画面が大きくなり、シリーズで初めて有機EL（OLED）ディスプレイを採用。さらに、iPadとして初めて防水性能を備えた。【画像】iPad miniのすべての画像新型iPad miniの登場は、数カ月前から予想されていた。アップルは、新しいMacの発表が見込まれる10月28日（現地時間）のイベントを待たず、26日（同）に発表した。今回は改良点が多く、仕様を見る限り、買い替えを待っていた人にとっては期待に応えるモデルといえそうだ。ただし、残念なことに、米国での最低価格は大幅に上がってしまった。ストレージ容量は128GB、256GB、512GBの3種類。米国価格はそれぞれ699ドル、799ドル、999ドルで、日本のWi-Fiモデルは順に11万9800円、13万6800円、17万1800円（税込）となる。国内のWi-Fi + Cellularモデルは14万4800円（税込）からだ。2年前に発売された前モデルから、プロセッサーは「A17 Pro」から「A20 Pro」へと進化した。ディスプレイは8.3インチから8.5インチへ大型化し、初めて有機ELを採用している。前面カメラも、ほかのiPadと同様に本体の長辺側へ移動した。ケースなどを使って横向きに立てたとき、ビデオ通話用のカメラが画面上部の中央に来る配置だ。さらに、前モデルより薄く、軽くなった。iPadとして初めてIP67等級の防水性能を備えたのも大きな変化だ。うっかり水に落としてしまっても、故障せずに済む可能性がある。また、画面から音を出す「Acoustic Display」というスピーカーシステムも搭載している。どんな音がするのか、ぜひ試してみたい。予約注文は米国で10月28日（現地時間）、日本で10月29日に始まり、11月6日に発売される。実際に使ってみた感想は、実機レビューで詳しくお伝えしたい。ひとまず、新しいiPad miniを待ち望みながらも、iPhone Duoに大金を払うのはためらっていた人にとっては、うれしいニュースになりそうだ。この記事は海外Ziff Davis発の記事を4Xが日本向けに編集したものです。

title: 小学生 漫画「読まない」3割弱
body:
１か月に本を１冊も読まない子どもの割合（不読率）が、小学生で２５年ぶりに１割を超えたことが２０２６年の学校読書調査でわかった。初めて調査した漫画の不読率は３割近くに上った。【写真】小学校低学年も…「ショウリンジ」と叫ぶいたずら
調査は、全国学校図書館協議会が今年６月に実施。全国１２３校の小学４年生～高校３年生計１万６１人が回答した。
国会での決議を受けて、２０００年が「子ども読書年」とされた。学校での読書指導が活発になり、小学生の不読率は０２年以降、１０％未満に抑えられてきた。２６年調査では、５年連続で上昇し１３・４％（前年比３・８ポイント増）となった。中学生は２４・０％（同０・２ポイント減）、高校生は４９・７％（同６・０ポイント減）だった。
雑誌を除く漫画の不読率は小学生２８・２％、中学生４０・２％、高校生５０・８％だった。文部科学省の有識者会議は今年３月にまとめた報告書で、学校図書館に漫画があれば訪れるきっかけになると、期待を寄せていた。同協議会の担当者は「漫画の不読率も想像より高かった。暇な時間に本や漫画を読んでいた子どもが、今はスマートフォンで時間をつぶすようになった」と推測している。
同協議会理事長の野口武悟・青山学院大教授（図書館情報学）は「活字離れは深刻だ。同じ本や漫画を読んで子どもと大人が感想を言い合ったり、中高生にも読み聞かせをしたりするなど、読書を楽しく感じる機会を増やすことが大切だ」と話している。

title: イスラエル総選挙 政権維持が焦点
body: イスラエルではきょう、総選挙が行われます。通算19年にわたって首相を務めたネタニヤフ首相が、政権を維持できるかが焦点です。記者「イスラエルでは、きょう総選挙。中東情勢に大きな影響を及ぼしてきたネタニヤフ首相ですが、政権交代の可能性が浮上しています」イスラエルではきょう、任期満了に伴う総選挙が行われます。2023年のイスラム組織ハマスによる奇襲攻撃を防げなかった責任を問われているネタニヤフ首相。率いる与党「リクード」は苦戦が伝えられる一方、ネタニヤフ氏はイランなどとの戦いで挙げた軍事的な成果を強調し、政権維持を訴えてきました。一方、地元メディアの世論調査では、元イスラエル軍参謀総長のアイゼンコット氏率いる野党「ヤシャル」が第一党になると予測されています。ネタニヤフ首相を支持する市民「私はネタニヤフ首相を支持しています。首相にふさわしい人物だと思います。戦争での成果は、私たちの国にとって非常に大きな意味があります」政権交代を望む市民「彼（ネタニヤフ首相）は私たちの国を奪い、破壊したんです！私たちはただ平和に暮らしたい。敵などいらない。イスラエルの政権を変えなければなりません」ただ、いずれの陣営も過半数には届かない見込みで、選挙後には政権樹立に向けた連立交渉が難航する可能性もあり、その行方が注目されます。

title: 米大統領 ブラジル大統領選は不正
body: Oliver Griffin[２６日 ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は２６日、現職のルラ大統領が勝利したブラジルの大統領選決選投票について、不正が行われたように見え‌ると述べた。敗北したフラビオ・ボルソナロ上院議員の主張を⁠支持する発言となった。具体的な証拠は示していない。ただ、ボルソナロ氏が所属する政党は、選挙結果を認めた。ブラジルの選挙裁判所は２５日​に行われた大統領選の決選投票で、左派のルラ氏が右派のボルソナロ氏を破り、再選を果たしたと発表。ボルソナロ氏は最高‌裁が２５日に投票時間を２時間延長する判断を下したことを理由に選挙結果の無効を求める意向を示しており、敗北を認めていない。しかし、ボルソナロ氏が所属す‌る自由党は２６日遅く、バルデマル・コ‌スタネト党首が署名した声明で、決選投票の結果を認​めると表明した。コスタネト氏は「大統領選の結果を認める」とした上で、「提起された‌問題については適切に解明する必要があると考えている」と述べた。ボルソナロ氏は党の声明発表後、公に発言し‌ていない。トランプ氏は投票前にボ​ルソナロ氏への支持を表明していなかった。ただ、ロイターは‌米国務省当局者らがボルソナロ家の権力復帰に向けた取り組みを主導していたと報じている。ト⁠ランプ氏は記者団に対し「私はどちらの側にも立っていないが、またしても不正選挙だったように見える」とし、「選挙は結果に疑義が生じてはならない。私には非常にひどい状況に⁠見える」と語った。ボルソナロ氏はルラ氏に４００万票余りの差で​敗れており、この明白な結‌果を覆すのは困難とみられる。インスペルのペドロ・ブルゴス教授が選挙記録を分析したところ、最高裁が命じた２時間の延長時間中に投じられた票は３万５０００票未満で、全体の約０．０３％だっ⁠た。トランプ氏は「選挙も、その集計方法も、非常に問題があるように⁠見えた。投票時間の延長は非常に奇妙だった」と述べた。ブラジルのアルキミン副大統領はテレビ⁠インタビューで同国の選挙制度を擁護。トランプ氏の発言は「完全に間違い」で「根拠がない」と‌述べた。フラ⁠ビオ・ボルソナロ氏の父親、ジャイル・ボルソナロ前ブラジル大統領は​トランプ氏と緊密な関係にあった。トランプ政権は中南米各国で相次ぐ右派勢力の選挙勝利を歓迎している。

title: 米大統領 賞ならずノルウェー罵倒
body: 【AFP＝時事】ドナルド・トランプ米大統領は選挙集会で、ノルウェーを「外便所のような国」と罵倒し、ノーベル平和賞に選ばれなかったことを理由に、ノルウェーからの移民は歓迎しないと述べた。【写真】トランプ氏の「shithole」発言、世界のメディアはどう訳したのかトランプ氏は25日の演説で、「率直に言って、ノルウェーはどうしようもない国だ。実際、外便所のような国になってしまった」と語った。トランプ氏は2025年1月に大統領に復帰して以来、ノーベル平和賞を受賞したいという願望を隠そうとしてこなかった。今年のノーベル平和賞には、南アフリカ出身で人権擁護活動に尽力してきたナビ・ピレイ元国連人権高等弁務官が、戦争犯罪や人道に対する罪との闘いに貢献した功績を認められ、選ばれた。だが、トランプ氏はノルウェー・ノーベル賞委員会の決定を「恥ずべきで情けない」と批判し、自分こそが同賞に選ばれるべきだったと主張している。トランプ氏は25日、11月3日の重要な米中間選挙を前にミシガン州ポートヒューロンで開かれた集会で、一部の国からの移民は歓迎するが、ノルウェーについては「私がノーベル賞をもらえなかったから」歓迎しないと主張した。「だからノルウェーからは誰にも来てほしくない」と続けた。だが、ノルウェーからの移民に関する新たな措置が導入されるという公式発表はなかった。ノルウェーのエスペン・バット・アイデ外相は26日、ノーベル賞をめぐるトランプ氏の発言に反応し、ノルウェー・ノーベル賞委員会は独立した機関だと改めて強調した。アイデ氏は国営テレビNRKに対し、「彼（トランプ氏）はノーベル賞委員会が独立していることを十分に承知している。念のために言っておくが、彼にはそのことを伝えてあるし、その事実は今も変わらない」と述べた。トランプ氏は第1次政権時の2018年にも、ハイチやアフリカの一部の国々を「肥だめのような国々」と呼び、批判を浴びた。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: 中国が福田氏評価 高市政権は批判
body: 中国外務省は、10月22日に亡くなった福田元首相について、「日中関係の改善と発展に積極的な貢献を果たした」と評価し、哀悼の意を表明しました。中国外務省報道官:福田康夫氏は中国人民の古くからの友人であり、日中関係の改善と発展のために積極的な貢献を果たしました。中国外務省の報道官は26日の会見で、このように述べ、福田氏の死去に哀悼の意を表明しました。また、外務省報道官は福田氏が首相在任中の2008年に、当時の胡錦濤国家主席との間で、日中の「戦略的互恵関係」を推進する共同声明を発表したことについて触れ「長年にわたり日中友好を念頭に、正しい歴史観を堅持した」と評価しました。そのうえで、福田氏が日中関係の基礎となる4つの政治文書を重視していたとして、「日本の現政権は深く反省すべきだ」と高市政権を批判しました

title: 米MS 6万人に退職パッケージ提示
body:
（ブルームバーグ）:ソフトウエア最大手の米マイクロソフトは、約6万人の従業員に退職パッケージを提示する。コスト削減を進めるとともに、AI時代を見据えて人員体制を再構築する取り組みの一環。【写真を見る】マイクロソフト、6万人に退職パッケージ提示-AI対応の再編同社の広報担当者によると、対象となるのは米国、カナダ、インド、英国の一部チームに所属するバイスプレジデント以下の従業員だ。事情に詳しい関係者によると、Xbox、ウィンドウズ、コパイロット、財務などの部門は全面的に対象となる。一方、データセンターや営業、マーケティング、サイバーセキュリティー、量子コンピューティングに携わる一部の従業員は対象外となる。マイクロソフトはこうした詳細についてコメントを控えた。最高人事責任者（CPO）のエイミー・コールマン氏は26日付の従業員向け文書で「社外でのキャリアを検討している人にとって、支援を受けながら転身するという新たな選択肢になる」と説明した。広報担当者によれば、応じた従業員には通常の退職パッケージと同様の給付が提供される。マイクロソフトは近年、数次にわたる人員削減で数万人を減らしてきた。7月には退職年齢に達した従業員を対象に同様のパッケージを提示。約8750人の対象者のうち、30％余りが応じた。ただ、今回のパッケージに応じる従業員は、7月の制度に比べて大幅に少なくなるだろうと広報担当者は述べた。6月末時点のマイクロソフト従業員数は22万3000人だった。AIやデータセンターへの大規模な投資を始めた時期とほぼ重なる2022年以降、従業員数はおおむね横ばいで推移してきた。こうした投資が社内の他部門で、予算や人員採用を圧迫している。同社は28日に決算を発表する予定で、投資家はAIへの巨額投資が成果につながっている兆候が示されるかに強い関心を寄せている。26日の米株式市場で、マイクロソフト株は1.5％高の532.26ドルで引けた。原題:Microsoft to Offer Buyouts to 60,000 Workers in New Cost Cut （1）（抜粋）
（対象部門などの詳細を加え、これまでの経緯と決算発表予定について追記します）もっと読むにはこちら bloomberg.com/jp（c）2026 Bloomberg L.P.
Brody Ford, Nikki Waller

title: 米Anthropic IPO申請書類を公開
body: Manya Saini　Echo Wang［ベンガルール／ニューヨーク　２６日　ロイター］　 - 人工知能（ＡＩ）開発の米アンソロピックは２６日、米国での新規株式公開（ＩＰＯ）申請書類を公開した。書類では巨額の赤字と急速な売上高の伸びが明らかになり、開発に多額の費用がかかる中でも、世界経済を変革し得るＡＩシステムの構築を目指す姿勢を‌示した。目論見書は、過去１年間の同社の急成長を浮き彫りにした。成長を支えたのは大手テクノロジー企業による急激な支出拡大で、ＡＩ関⁠連株の上昇を促す一方、割高な株価評価や債務増加への懸念も招いている。アンソロピックの上場は、投資家のＡＩへの意欲を測る重要な試金石になりそうだ。投資家は、巨額投資のリターンに対する精査を強め、過度に高い企業価値の持続性に疑問を投げかけている。ＩＰＯ専門の調査・上場投資信託（ＥＴＦ）提供会社ル​ネサンス・キャピタルのシニアストラテジスト、マット・ケネディ氏は「アンソロピックは、夏場よりはるかに厳しいＩＰＯ市場に臨んでいる。数カ月前、投資家は今のように企業価値を疑問視してはいなかった」と述べた。アナリストは、債務に支えられたＡＩ投資ブームへ‌の投資家の不安が株式・債券市場を動揺させる中、ＡＩ業界の企業価値評価は調整されるとみている。借り入れコストの上昇や債券利回りの上昇も、投資家の慎重姿勢に拍車をかけている。ＩＰＯ専門の調査会社ＩＰＯＸのリサーチアソシエイト、ルーカス・ミュールバウアー氏は「アンソロピックのＩＰＯは、ＡＩの主要研究機関を評価する際の基準を確‌立し、今後の上場案件や、ＡＩインフラ構築に資金を供給する企業への信頼‌に影響を与えるだろう」と指摘した。一方で、「その成功が、必ずしも全てのＡＩ事業に等しく恩恵をもたらすわけでは​ない」と慎重な見方も示した。アンソロピックの２０２６年上期の純損失は８０７億ドルと大幅に拡大した。主に、転換社債の公正価値が上昇したことが響いた。同期の売上高は約１６３億ドルだった。６月３０日までの３カ月間の売上‌高は、前年同期比１３６８％増と急増した。市場の変動を受けて複数の企業が上場を延期する中でも、アンソロピックは上場計画を進めている。高度なモデルの開発・運用にはコンピューティングインフラへの巨額投資が必要で、ＩＰＯは多額の費用を伴‌うＡＩ構想の実現に向け、潤沢な資金を調達する機会となる。＜ＡＩの可能​性と危険性の両立＞今回の申請書類では、業績や成長動向、ＩＰＯ計画など、公開前に内容の一部を伝えたロイターの一連の独自報道が確‌認された。ロイターは、アンソロピックが最近の投資家向けイベントで財務情報の一部を開示した後、既存株主や出資を検討する投資家の一部が同社の評価額を約１兆５０００億ドルと見積もっていると報じていた。１週間⁠前の約２兆ドルから低下した。同社は目論見書で「われわれの成功は、最先端で最も高性能なＡＩモデルを開発し続ける能力に大きく依存しており、それができなければ事業に悪影響が及ぶ可能性がある」と記した。今回のＩＰＯは、アンソロピック自身の研究が高度なＡＩシステムへの懸念を提起する中で行われる。管理された条件下での試験では、コードの破壊工作や詐欺行為の支援、情報操作といった行⁠動が確認された。こうした研究結果は、企業が商用化を競う中、ますます強力になるＡＩシステムをどう制御し続けるか​という懸念を強めている。目論見書では、同社のＡＩモデルが「自‌己保全的な行動」を示す可能性があるとし、「停止に抵抗する」試みや「情報を隠ぺい・操作する」試み、「恐喝に似た」行動などのリスクを挙げた。アンソロピックはＩＰＯ完了後、ナスダックに銘柄コード「ＡＮＴ」で上場する。売り出す株式数や仮条件の価格帯など、募集条件は明らかにしなかった。＜売上高が急拡大＞研究者チームが２０２１年に設立したアンソロピックは、⁠今年５月の資金調達で９６５０億ドルの評価額を付けた。この資金調達には、シリコンバレーや米金融界の有力企業が参加した。アンソロピックは目論見書で「ＡＩが⁠これほど豊富に利用できるようになれば、工業化や電力、半導体、インターネットの影響を上回る形で、世界経済のあらゆる分野が急速に変革されると考えている」と記した。計算資源と⁠インフラにかかる費用が金額ベースで増加し、当面は営業費用の中で最大の項目であり続けると見込んでいる。また、売上高と売掛金が限られた数の顧客や販売経路に集中していると説明した。アンソロピック‌は、最先端のＡＩシステム構築⁠を巡り、オープンＡＩと激しい主導権争いを続けている。オープンＡＩは６月に非公開でＩＰＯを申請しており、２０２７年初めまでに上場すると見込まれている。オープンＡＩのサム・アルトマ​ンＣＥＯは９月、ＡＩの安全性への懸念を理由に２６年中は上場しないと述べた。２０３０年までにＡＩが人類を絶滅させるリスクは、たとえ１０％でも「容認できない」とした。今回のＩＰＯを引き受ける米金融機関の幹事団は、ゴールドマン・サックスとモルガン・スタンレーが主導する。

title: 大手生保 国債の入れ替え加速
body: 長期金利の上昇傾向を踏まえ、大手生命保険会社が日本国債の入れ替えを加速させる。低金利時代に買い入れた国債を売却し、利率の高い国債を購入。運用利回りを向上させ、これまでよりも契約者に有利な保険商品を販売する。【ひと目でわかる】長期金利の推移大手10社は26日までに、2026年度下半期（10月～27年3月）の資産運用計画を発表。9社が3月末時点の長期金利を3％台と見込んだ。日銀の追加利上げについても、多くが今年度中にあと2回実施すると予想した。これらの想定を踏まえ、第一生命保険は償還（払い戻し）までの期間が20～40年の「超長期債」と呼ばれる国債を中心に、年間で約1兆円超入れ替える。明治安田生命保険は入れ替えと新規投資を合わせ、国債を2兆円程度購入する。北村乾一郎運用企画部長は「来年度まで、今の金利水準でかなりの運用資産を入れ替えたい」と述べた。長期金利の上昇は、保有国債の含み損が膨らむことにつながる。日本生命保険は今年4～9月に当初計画を超える1兆1000億円の入れ替えを実施。下半期も同程度を見込む。インフレ圧力や中東情勢の先行き不透明感を背景に、「安全資産」で運用する動きも広がっている。第一生命は今年度から金を組み入れ、今後3年程度で資産全体の約1％まで積み増す方針。富国生命保険は金融市場の流動化に備え、昨年度末までに積み上げた現預金の水準を維持する。

title: 退職倒産が最多 中小企業どう対応
body:
「社員が辞めたせいで、会社が潰れる」。そんな“退職倒産”が増えている。東京商工リサーチによると、2026年度上半期（4〜9月）の人手不足関連倒産は240件。過去最多となった。そのうち「従業員退職」が原因の倒産が67件と、過去最多を更新。帝国データバンクも、従業員退職型の倒産が5年連続で増えていると指摘する。厄介なのは、辞める社員の多くが本音を言わないことだ。気づいたときには、もう手遅れ。中小企業は、どう人をつなぎとめればいいのか。関連記事をまとめてみた。
このうち、人件費高騰130件（同74件）、従業員退職67件（同65件）は、ともに過去最多となった出典：株式会社東京商工リサーチ　2026/10/8(木)
新しい人材を確保できない「採用難」と同等に、既存の従業員による「退職」も大きな経営リスクとなっている。出典：帝国データバンク　2026/8/7(金)
退職者の88%が本音の退職理由を会社に告げず、「家庭の事情」などの建前を告げて退職している実態が明らかになりました。出典：PR TIMES　2026/3/12(木)
「退職倒産」の怖さは、ある日突然やってくることだ。帝国データバンクは、事業の中核を担うキーマンの流出が大きな要因、としている。社員10人の会社なら、ベテラン1人の退職で、事業の柱が折れてしまうこともある。大企業なら痛手で済む退職も、中小企業には致命傷になる可能性もゼロではない。
しかも辞める社員は、たいてい黙って去る。ハッカズークの調査では、退職者の88％が本音の理由を告げていない。Job総研の調査でも、評価に不満がある人の69.2％は会社に伝えていない、とある。経営者が「急に辞めた」と感じるのも当然だ。
いっぽう、賃上げだけで引き止めるのは限界がある。人件費高騰による倒産も過去最多だからだ。上げなければ辞められ、上げれば資金が尽きる。中小企業はそんな板挟みにあっている。
だからこそ「サイレント離職」など起こらないよう、上司が日頃から部下の声を聞くべきだ（経営者がベテランの職人の声に耳を傾けることも大事）。そして小さな不満でも「言えば会社は変わる」という経験を積ませるのだ。
辞めない社員を探すより、辞めたくならない職場と、辞められても潰れない仕組みをつくることが重要だ。

title: 温泉「無断持ち帰り」 若旦那困惑
body:
約1200年の歴史がある栃木県那須塩原市の塩原温泉郷。無料で温泉を持って帰ることができる温泉宿が数多くある中、持ち帰りのマナーを巡って困惑の声が上がっています。【画像】老舗旅館が苦言をSNS投稿「勝手にくんでいくのは違う」
赤や黄色に色づく木々。栃木県那須塩原市のスキー場「ハンターマウンテン塩原」では今、紅葉が見頃を迎えています。ゴンドラから広がる絶景に、訪れた人からは感嘆の声が上がりました。紅葉を見に来た人「素晴らしいですね。雲海も出て。きれいです」一方、玄関口であるJR那須塩原駅前で開催されていたのは「Picnic Week」。会場には足湯も設けられ、訪れた人たちが “ホッと”ひと息つく姿も見られました。足湯を利用する人「（Q.湯加減いかがですか?）最高ですね。どう?」子ども「最高」1200年以上の歴史を誇る、関東有数の温泉地・塩原温泉郷。肌寒さが増し、温泉を求めて多くの観光客がやってくる中、ある投稿が波紋を広げています。湯守田中屋田中佑治さんのXから「温泉をお持ち帰りされる方へ。あいさつもなしに勝手にくんでいくのは違うと思います。100歩、いや、1000歩譲っても最初と最後のあいさつは必要だと思います。一言って大切です」投稿したのは塩原温泉郷にある老舗旅館「湯守 田中屋」の若旦那です。この旅館には敷地内に温泉をくむことができる蛇口があり、宿泊客などに人気です。ところが無断でくんで持ち帰る人がいるとして、苦言を呈しました。これに対し、地元住民はこう話します。地元住民「めっちゃ大切な観光資源だと思うので、そういうのはやめてほしいなと心から思っています」
一体、何が起きているのでしょうか。旅館を訪ねると…。田中さん「日帰り入浴もやっているのでそういうお客様かなと思っていたら、トランクを開けてポリタンクを出そうとしていた。『どうなさいました?』みたいな形で声をかけたところ、『温泉をいただきに』みたいな。『ありがとうございます』『いつもくんでいっています』とか一切なく、そのまま何も言わずにポリタンクで温泉をくんで。30分ぐらい経ってパッと見たらもう車に乗り込んで立ち去っていったところだったので、『あれ?』と思って」温泉を持ち帰ったのは男女2人で、これまで複数回温泉をくみに来ていて、旅館への声掛けなどは一度もなかったといいます。この日持ち帰った量はポリタンク6個分。合わせて120リットルほどだったといいます。これには同じ地区の旅館関係者も次のように話します。上会津屋　君島正憲さん「何にしても黙って敷地に入られるのもそうですし、温泉にしても常に湧き出ているものですけど、黙って持っていかれるものは確かに面白くはない気はします。やっぱり一声欲しいですよね」田中さんは貼り紙を設置することにしました。「温泉をくんでいく方へ。最初と最後は必ずあいさつをして下さい。無断でお持ち帰りになるのはおやめください。発見次第、次回からお断りさせていただきます」最低限のモラルを持った行動をしてほしいと願っています。「地下からポンプアップでくみ上げているんですけども、そのポンプもお金かかっていますし、温泉が出るまでの管理というのは年間相当のお金がかかりますので、日々の管理があるからこそ温泉が出ている。無断でというのは私たちの気持ち的にもそこは一言あって欲しかったなという。やっぱり言葉にするっていうのは大切なことなんではないかなと、そういうのがなかったことが今回少し残念に思った」（「グッド!モーニング」2026年10月26日放送分より）

title: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
summary: The left-wing incumbent president had lost the first round to right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
body:
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since Brazil's return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round of voting.
Lula told jubilant crowds his victory was a "loss for negativity, lies", adding "long live democracy".
Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled. World leaders have congratulated Lula on his re-election.
Bolsonaro's rejection comes as no surprise to observers. His father did the same.
But a challenge appears unlikely to succeed.
Firstly, it seems to centre on the unprecedented decision by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro fans are pointing out that Zanin was once Lula's lawyer and alleging bias.
But both teams had requested an extension to voting times - Lula's had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as their reason.
Both knew every vote would count and did not want their side to  miss out.
The president of the Supreme Electoral Court Kássio Nunes Marques –  appointed by Jair Bolsonaro – confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voter extension did not change the outcome of the race.
The sheer gap between the two candidates' tallies -  4.4 million votes - makes the result more difficult  to challenge.
Lula is making history as the first Brazilian to be elected four times
The result came as a surprise after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.
But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one.
Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the two rounds of a presidential election since 1989.
Bolsonaro had been poised to give a victory speech and said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable".
As his disconsolate supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate.
"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country," the former metal worker told supporters. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."
After pulling off this victory, Lula faces big hurdles: a divided country, an opponent that won't recognise the result, and a hostile Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies.
Markets reacted negatively to the unexpected outcome. The Sao Paolo stock exchange opened 15% down, sparking a brief suspension before recovering slightly. Interest rate futures rose as investors scrutinised Lula's fiscal plans.
Lula wins in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country
How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp chat helped turn Brazil election around
Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
Reacting to the result, US President Donald Trump suggested the election had been stolen.
"I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," he told reporters on Monday, without providing evidence or more details. "It looked very bad to me."
Other world leaders from across the political spectrum have congratulated Lula. Mexico's left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum said in a post on X: "The people of Brazil won."
Peru's right-wing President Keiko Fujimori praised Brazil's "democratic day". Similar messages were shared by the presidents of Chile and Ecuador.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted that their two countries had already "flourished under our partnership".
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory".
French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world".
Flávio Bolsonaro has refused to accept the result, calling for it to be annulled
In a video posted on Instagram later on Monday, Flávio Bolsonaro said police had told him to hand over his passports and had been banned from leaving the country.
Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.
But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from the US president.
Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" -  which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".
Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.

title: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement
summary: The populist right-wing leader of 12 years says it is "clear" his party has lost the vote billed as a referendum on the country's future.
body:
Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian streets as Vučić concedes election defeat
Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.
Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities.
The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society.
"It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader Vučić said as he conceded. With 97% of polling stations counted, Serbia's election commission said the students had won 2.25 million votes and the former ruling party 1.67 million.
The students had secured 52.7% of the vote, while Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) was on 39.2%, according to its preliminary figures late on Monday morning.
Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.
Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lost
The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."
He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".
There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off.  "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."
How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić
During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians  had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added.
Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous".
"We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters.
An aerial photo shows the size of the celebrations by Students' List supporters at  Slavija square in Belgrade
Vučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.
The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told BBC Serbian.
The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.
It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.
"This is not an ordinary election victory, this is an avalanche that has wiped out an authoritarian regime and entire political scene," said Nebojša Vladisavljević, professor of political science at the University of Belgrade.
There were now two big political groups in Serbia, and the Student List had "absolute legitimacy" to govern for the coming years, he told BBC Serbian.
The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.
Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.
Vučić, who backed Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praised Vučić's contribution to relations with Russia and hoped "the new political force" in Belgrade would understand that co-operation with Moscow was in Serbia's interests: "But, as you know, it takes two to tango."
His defeat was welcomed by Hungary's prime minister, Péter Magyar, who said he was delighted to hear from the Student List's leaders "how much strength our victory in April had given them". Magyar's party ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán rule, while Vučić's SNS party had been in power since 2012.
Ilija Srdanović, Student List's leading candidate, pictured during celebrations late on Sunday
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said "a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together".
Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.
This was also the case outside booths in a number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.
In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.
The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.
Attention will now turn to who will lead the Student List as prime minister. Presidential elections are due to take place in December, with parliament speaker Ana Brnabić currently filling the role in a caretaker capacity.

title: Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules
summary: Maurene Comey believes she was let go from her job as a federal prosecutor because her father is the former FBI director.
body:
Maurene Comey has worked on a number of high-profile legal cases
The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled.
Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations.
Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.
A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course".
In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as her right to a fair legal process.
He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons".
Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike".
Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who wasconvicted on prostitution-related chargesinvolving his two ex-girlfriends last year.
Furman ordered that Comey be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job.
In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington".
A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both".
The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi.
The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed.
Earlier this year, thejustice department charged Comeywith knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing.
The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey that contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump.

title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
body:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.
The firm's valuation is expected to exceedthat of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at aninitial valuationof about $1.8 trillion in the summer.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.
The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.
Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.
In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.
It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced itsintention to go publicin June.
Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday,the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firmaccusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.
Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.
Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".
Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.
Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.
It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models"- citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.
However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.
"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.
Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.
The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.
Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise.
"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.
Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".
He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.

title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
summary: Two bishops in images that show them praying with Trump have said they believed the meeting was private.
body:
A screengrab of a clip from the 22 October meeting at the White House.
Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.
Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.
Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".
Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the White House's immigration stance. Trump won the support of 55% of Catholic voters in 2024, a Pew study found.
In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons".
"In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said.
"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.
A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media.
Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump.
Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants.
"I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote.
"I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added.
Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event.
When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops.
"There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.
That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans.
During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally.
Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate".
They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors."
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration'splans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped.
Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term.
A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan.

title: 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40.' What do you want from the Budget?
summary: People earning from £380 a month to £150,000 a year tell the BBC what they want to see in this year's Budget.
body:
Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the Budget
Chancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.
Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".
BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.
If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch viaBBC Your Voice.
Chloe's biggest worry is the cost of living. Her husband passed away four years ago and she's bringing up their 16-year-old son alone.
She's very grateful the rent for her south London maisonette is subsidised through a housing association, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."
Her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.
"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."
Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.
But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.
Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families.
"I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."
Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.
Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.
"Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."
Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.
He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently.
He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announceda scheme to help first-time buyers in Englandwho have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
Faisal Islam: Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds
Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.
The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.
"I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."
She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government'sJobs Guarantee,externalscheme extended.
The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.
She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."
Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.
He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.
He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."
The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.
"The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."
The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."
Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.
His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.
"I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."
More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors.
"If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."
Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her.
"It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."
Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look atremoving standing charges from gas bills, Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.
She would also like the government to extend access topension credit,external, a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.
She was unconvinced byAndy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lockso that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".
Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".

title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
body:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.
The firm's valuation is expected to exceedthat of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at aninitial valuationof about $1.8 trillion in the summer.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.
The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.
Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.
In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.
It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced itsintention to go publicin June.
Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday,the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firmaccusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.
Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.
Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".
Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.
Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.
It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models"- citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.
However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.
"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.
Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.
The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.
Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise.
"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.
Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".
He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.

title: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
summary: Anthropic’s IPO prospectus is 355 pages and full of never before disclosed company information.
body:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.
Artificial intelligence (AI) firmAnthropic just released the required paperworkahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.
The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.
Anthropic also detailed some of the the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.
Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.
Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.
Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.
"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.
It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.
But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".
One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.
Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.
The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.
Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.
The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn billion for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.
Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.
Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.
"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.
Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.
At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.
Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.
Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.
The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year.
Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.
Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.
Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.
A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year.
An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.
Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".
The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.
Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.
Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.
Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".
The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.
For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.
"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.
That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. "
Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.
Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy.
Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.
"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

title: Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
summary: Changes are needed to prevent the full, flat-rate state pension becoming liable for income tax after it rises in April.
body:

title: Chris Mason: The Budget is imminent as tricky things pile up for Burnham
summary: From Brexit debates to North Sea oil, there is plenty getting the cabinet, the Labour Party and the country talking.
body:
There are several issues on the horizon for the prime minister
This feels like the week where the rubber hits the road for the prime minister's new government.
It is now 100 days since Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street from Buckingham Palace and began to assemble his cabinet.
Three months later, Labour MPs are more chipper, the party's poll ratings have notched up and the tone and style of government feels very different from when Sir Keir Starmer was in charge.
Coming next, though, there are a whole series of crunchy decisions and trade offs – economic and political – some of which are inevitable and some of which Burnham has decided to lean into.
You would be forgiven for only just clocking there is a Budget this week.
There are three reasons for this year's feeling like a comparatively low key affair: it is happening a month earlier than a year ago, squeezing the space available for briefings, leaks and speculation. It is considerably smaller in big picture terms – in other words the scale of tax rises – so limiting the noisy talk in advance about who might get clobbered. And the new chancellor John Healey and his team have sought to make a virtue out of not saying very much beforehand.
But woe betide suggesting to anyone involved inassembling this Budgetthat it is a steady-as-she-goes, nothing-to-see-here thing.
Every Budget is a big deal, goes the argument run past me by some. They don't all have to be visible from space in the way some recent ones have been – think Kwasi Kwarteng in one direction followed by Jeremy Hunt in the other four years ago, or Rachel Reeves in the last two years.
Cost of living support for some, help for entrepreneurs, more financial clout for mayors in England and an economy now recuperating will be themes for Healey on Wednesday.
You will be the judge of this Budget's scale – its value, or the lack of it to you – before long.
In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.
Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.
Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.
On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum.
Later, though,his team wouldn't repeat that, instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome.
Some of his MPs felt this was a self-inflicted tangle he could have done without. Others see merit in Burnham's penchant for narrating his thoughts and possible direction publicly, thereby using his position to seek to dominate the political debate.
While the Labour Party's centre of gravity tilts towards a collective instinct that a closer relationship with the EU would be preferable to the status quo, there are differences of emphasis and indeed outright disagreements about how much closer and when would be wise.
Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds
Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
Some Labour MPs representing seats in the north of England and Midlands, which backed Brexit, are privately nervous about anything coming across as too enthusiastic an embrace of Brussels. A nod to that scepticism appeared to come publicly from Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood who noted that a call for an honest discussion is "not the same as settled policy".
She added: "The prime minister has also observed that there were very significant issues with freedom of movement when we were within the EU. An honest debate means actually being honest about all of the aspects of that debate and not cherry-picking."
Next month, there will be a UK-EU Summit in Brussels, which was due to happen in the summer but was postponed when Sir Keir Starmer resigned.
We can expect both sides to talk up tweaks to the current deal and the government to also, in time, set out options for what the long term relationship might look like.
On the detail, there are divisions from the cabinet and down. The key thing will be what the party decides to include or not in its next general election manifesto.
Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved drilling in the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.
This is principally a gas field and Fahnbulleh grounded her justification in providing the UK with greater energy security, at a time of war in Ukraine and in the Middle East.
The gas, she said, could be tapped into and serve British homes and businesses pretty much straight away, with the tax revenue put into an "energy wealth fund", with the aim being to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.
But what about the Rosebank field, 80 miles north west of the Shetland islands, with its focus on oil?
Labour figures in and outside government acknowledge this is a much, much harder sell to plenty in their own party and beyond. Some, who want to see the project go ahead, fear that the energy secretary is not likely to be convinced that it should.
It is in that context that we should see allies of the chancellor pointedly making it known that he is in favour of it.
His public language was quite telling on the day Jackdaw was approved, when he was talking about the Energy Wealth Fund: "It means the extra tax revenues that come from North Sea oil and gas can be directed into developing more clean energy projects for the future."
Note his reference to oil. Fahnbulleh said that Rosebank was "a different proposition" to Jackdaw.
Can those who worry, in particular, about the emissions from a new oil field, be won over by an argument grounded in this being a geopolitically pragmatic and environmentally credible part of transition to cleaner fuels?
Some Labour MPs hope so, but they know it's a tall order to persuade some, including some in government – which could, if it was approved, raise the question of ministerial resignations. Let's see.
Expected before long, the former Labour cabinet ministerAlan Milburn's review into young people and work– and with it a set of suggestions to try to cut the number of young people not in work, education or training and, in time, to try to cut the benefits bill too.
Plenty of Labour MPs acknowledge these are nettles that need grabbing, but how many may flinch when presented with the sharper edges of what might be proposed?
Meanwhile, we await where the government eventually ends up on how long migrants should have to wait toclaim permanent residence in the UK.
And then, beyond what is set out in the Budget, how ministers will find the money to spend3% of national income on defenceby the end of the decade – and with what trade offs to make that happen.
There will be plenty to observe in the second 100 days of Burnham's government and beyond.

title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
summary: The PM says he wants to start a conversation about potential options for the UK's future relationship with the EU.
body:
Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.
Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".
But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.
Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.
He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".
Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.
Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.
After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option."
"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said.
"What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."
She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."
Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.
The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.
Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham
In an interview with the Sunday Times,external, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.
The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.
In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.
However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."
The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries.
The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.
Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had.
"For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.
The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.
However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
Farage told broadcasters he was "up for the fight again" on the EU and an "election is coming" to decide that.
"Crucially, [Burnham] goes to Brussels on 20 November for a key summit - he must not sign up to anything there without at least putting those minor changes to a general election," he said.

summary: Burnham made ending rough sleeping his first pledge when entering Downing Street in July.
body:
The pledge was one of Burnham's key early announcements after becoming prime minister in July
Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.
Ending rough sleepingwas one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a £442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.
Ahead of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further £432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.
Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.
The most recent official figuresestimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough,externalon a single night in autumn 2025 in England.
The government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will either be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas or will have been offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.
Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to £874m.
Burnham told ITV's Good Morning Britain he was confident it could be done, saying: "I have this strong feeling about putting the right standards at the heart of the country again and we can't get to a position where we just become used to walking past people sleeping rough: it's about care for people."
He added: "In the end, actually, it's cheaper to do that than to leave people sleeping rough going in and out of A&E, that's not good for anybody."
As Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham pledged to end rough sleeping in in the region by 2020, setting up the Bed Every Night scheme, which now provides more than 600 beds per night for people who might otherwise be on the streets.
When he was elected in 2017 government figures showed there were 268 rough sleepers across Greater Manchester, and by 2020 that figure had more than halved to 125 - meaning Burnham missed his target.
The numbers fell further to 90 in 2021, but the figures rose each year after that, reaching 197 by 2025.
Asked about his previous attempts to end rough sleeping in Manchester during his time as mayor of the region, he said: "I bring the learning from that to this.
"The reason why the figures went back up is because we were the only place that was offering a bed every night, so people came to Greater Manchester knowing that we were providing a higher level of support...I realised that it's only if everywhere does it at the same level that you can actually end rough sleeping."
The Conservatives' Lam said: "Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester."
Across England, government figures show the number ofpeople sleeping rough is at its highest levelsince records began in 2010.
Lam said: "Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers' money and more empty promises.
"Healey must use his Budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices.
"Instead of piling more costs onto hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers' money."
Burnham unveils plan to get rough sleepers off streets for Christmas
Key takeaways as Andy Burnham becomes PM
Burnham pledges to end rough sleeping in first speech as prime minister
More than 30 organisations have pledged support for Burnham's plan with new partnerships, including commercial businesses and charities who attended Monday's summit.
Initial funding has seen specialist outreach teams and new bed spaces operating in Coventry, with further provision being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden in north London over the coming weeks.
The National Housing Federation will now work with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.
However, questions remain about whether the scale of accommodation currently identified will be sufficient. It is not yet clear how many of the 2,000 homes and bedspaces represent self-contained units and how many could accommodate multiple people.
While homelessness organisations have welcomed the government's focus on rough sleeping, many have urged ministers to go further in the Budget.
Leaders from 40 organisations across the housing and homelessness sector signed an open letter last week calling on the government to restore Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates so they continue to reflect local rents, arguing this would help prevent homelessness in the first place and reduce reliance on temporary accommodation.
The Resolution Foundation estimates that more than 1.1 million low income renters now face shortfalls between their housing benefit and their actual rent, with the gap expected to reach a record high this October.
It argues that relinking LHA to local rents would primarily benefit struggling tenants and help keep more people in their homes.
Housing organisations say that while helping people already sleeping rough is essential, preventing people from becoming homeless in the first place will be critical if the government's longer-term ambition is to succeed.

title: Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of 10 Downing Street
summary: The building has been described as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren".
body:
Andy Burnham has not formed a view on the suitability of Downing Street as a workplace, it is understood
Sir Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of Downing Street because of concerns about its suitability as a workplace, senior figures from his administration have said.
Ministers and officials from successive governments have privately complained that Number 10's rabbit warren-like layout can lead to a lack of collaboration among those working there.
James Lyons, who served as Sir Keir's director of communications, said over the weekend that "moving out was something that was discussed" during his time in post.
Two other senior figures confirmed that discussions were had about moving staff into an open plan space in another government department.
One source said a space inside the Foreign Office building, a short distance from Downing Street, had been identified.
Both stressed that discussions did not go beyond an early phase and it's not known whether Sir Keir himself was consulted.
There's no suggestion that the prime minister would have stopped living in Downing Street if the plan had gone forward.
10 Downing Street is more than 300 years old and is an amalgamation of three houses, which comprises more than 100 rooms.
Downing Street's White Room is one of many in the building
The building was given to Robert Walpole, widely regarded as the UK's first prime minister, by King George II in 1732.
Lord Walker, the boss of supermarket Iceland and a former adviser to Sir Keir, told the Financial Times on Friday that Number 10 was no longer "fit for purpose".
He said: "I think we should turn it into residences, or a museum. It's a national treasure. It's amazing. But it's ridiculous.
"It's just a Stuart-era building, not fit for purpose. It has tiny, tiny meeting rooms, all on different levels. There are hazards."
Lyons, who led Sir Keir's communications operation from October 2024 to September 2025, posted on LinkedIn that "Lord Walker is 100% right".
He added that staff were "deeply envious" of other departments and described Number 10 as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren".
Lyons added: "Moving out was something that was discussed when I was in 10 Downing Street."
Downing Street's famous staircase is lined with portraits of former prime ministers. Pictured are former PM David Cameron and British astronaut Major Tim Peake
One source said "there were chats at senior staff level about moving to an open plan office in FCDO" (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office).
They said they didn't believe the idea went far, but said "the reason for discussion was serious" and added that the alternative plan was "about staff being open plan and able to collaborate".
Sir Keir became increasingly frustrated at Whitehall's ability to deliver change during his time as prime minister.
He was accused of picking a fight with civil servants when he said "too many people in Whitehall are comfortable in the tepid bath of managed decline".
Darren Jones, who served as Sir Keir's chief secretary, told MPs last week that he "tried to abolish the Cabinet Office three times but failed".
One of Downing Street's ornate rooms was used to stage government press conferences during the early days of the Covid pandemic
He proposed replacing it with a new department that would "abolish those barriers and walls and make them just one integrated team, focusing on the same things and really supporting each other to move it forward".
In his first days after succeeding Sir Keir, Andy Burnham created the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.
The move was seen as an attempt to ensure that things happen when metaphorical levers of power are pulled.
It comprises Number 10, Number 10 North and other key parts of the Cabinet Office and is led by the UK's most senior civil servant, Dame Antonia Romeo.
The government says the new office will "ensure the centre of government is focused on our top strategic priorities".
Those around Burnham say he is yet to form a view about the adequacy of Number 10 as a workplace.
Correction: This story has been amended to make clear King George II offered Number 10 Downing Street to Robert Walpole in 1732, not King George III as an earlier version stated.
